msItem.incipit: Death's only terrible in the very name

abstract.p: The poem is an elegy for Dr Johnson that reflects on death while praising his exceptional virtue as a physician. It begins by minimizing the terror of death, likening it to sleep, before turning to a paradox: Death has destroyed its own “grand agent,” the physician, whose art ordinarily combats illness. The speaker contrasts the harm often attributed to medical practice with Johnson’s superior skill, presenting him as one who saved more lives than others destroyed. His death is explained as Death’s deliberate act to remove a force that opposed it. The poem concludes by lamenting the loss of a doctor who healed both body and mind, and whose integrity left him materially unrewarded, casting his honesty and selflessness as the defining features of his life.

div.head: On Dr Johnson a Physitian. November 1621

lg.l: Deaths only terrible in the very name
And some few circumstances, else ‘twere the same
To go to bed and dy, for do Death right
’Tis a sound sleepe, a little longer night:
Yea of some living deade men I have reade
Which Who each night died, and made theire Grave theire bedd.
Yet I must question Death, how hee now can
Kill his Grand Agent, A Physitian;
For Physicks a disease spoiles more by farr,
Then either Cooke, a Pestilence or Warre:
There are such skilfull Doctors in’t they say,
That they can kill theire thrice score a weeke, and Play.
But Johnsons art was nobler and sav’d more
Then twenty of deaths Instruments slew before;
Wherfore enrag’d to see men crosse his lawes,
To stopp th’effect hee takes away the cause,
And slayes Him first: and in him many one,
Who pine to see theire health before them gone.
Now hee is gone where shall a Patient finde
On that will cure his body and his Minde;
One both Whose arte and Toungue with a sweete jarr
Strove in each cure to out slipp the other farr:
Whose good to others hurt himselfe, and Which
Did live too honest to dy over rich.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Thomas Johnson (c.1578–1621) was a physician based in Oxford. The son of a Bedfordshire gentleman, he matriculated at St Alban Hall in 1594 aged sixteen, proceeding BA from Oriel College in 1596 and MA in 1601 (incorporated at Cambridge in 1604). He supplicated for a licence to practise medicine on 13 June 1608 and was awarded the degrees of Bachelor and Doctor of Medicine on 26 June 1609. He resided in the parish of St Mary Magdalen and was buried at St Mary the Virgin, Oxford, on 16 November 1621(Oxfordshire Medics)
